subtype: Approach: rehearsing how to explain the project to visitors [Action]
passage: Thursday night. Fair is on Saturday! Today I practised my one-minute talk in front of the mirror: what I asked (does a plant lean toward light?), what I did (bean plant by the window, box turned each day), what I found (it bent toward the glass in four days). 58 seconds. Then I made my sister Leela sit on the bed and fire the hardest questions she could think of. She asked, "Why didn't you use two plants?" and I froze for a whole breath. Now the answer is on a card. Leela was a pretty good judge and I told her so. 🙂 Tomorrow, once more with the card. - Nikhil

qa.q: How long did Nikhil's practice talk take?
How did Nikhil feel when Leela asked why Nikhil had not used two plants?
qa.a: Caught off guard and briefly worried; freezing for a whole breath shows the question was a surprise.

qa.q: What other way could Nikhil prepare for tricky questions, and why?
qa.a: Nikhil could ask a classmate to question the project too, since a different person may ask something Leela did not think of.

qa.q: What might Leela feel about her part in the practice?
qa.a: Leela probably enjoys playing the judge and is pleased that Nikhil praised the questions, since Nikhil told her she was good at it.

grounding: A child rehearses a one-minute talk of the question, method and finding, with a sister asking hard questions.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing how to explain the project to visitors [Action]
passage: In the small school at Wai, the science exhibition was on Saturday, and Dhruv's project was about how rainwater can be collected from roofs. He knew the model by heart, but when he tried to explain it to his mother, he rambled for five minutes. So he made a rule: one minute, three parts. What I wondered. What I did. What I found. He practised in the courtyard, timing himself with the kitchen clock. Then he asked his sister Esha to be a difficult judge. "Why a roof and not the ground?" "What if it doesn't rain?" "Is the water safe to drink?" He stumbled on that last one, so they worked out an honest answer together: "Not without cleaning." On Saturday, the real judge asked exactly that.

qa.q: How long did Dhruv want his explanation to be?
qa.a: Dhruv wanted it to be one minute.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when he stumbled on Esha's last question?
qa.a: He felt caught out and a little flustered, which is why he wanted to work out an answer before Saturday.

qa.q: What else could Dhruv practise, and why?
qa.a: He could practise saying "I don't know, but I would test it by...", because judges often ask things nobody has prepared for.

qa.q: How does being the difficult judge look to Esha?
qa.a: Esha enjoys the job and feels useful, since her tricky question turned out to be the real one.

grounding: It shows a boy practising a one-minute explanation of what he asked, did and found, and asking his sister to ask tricky questions.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing how to explain the project to visitors [Action]
passage: Chidi had built a small solar oven out of a pizza box for his school's science fair in Lisbon. The day before, he stood in the kitchen with a timer. "Question, method, result. One minute." His first try took three. His second took ninety seconds. His third was fifty-eight seconds. Then he turned to his sister. "Rafaela, be a mean judge." She folded her arms and put on a deep voice. "Why black paper inside?" "Why does foil help?" "Would it work in winter?" He didn't know the winter one, so he wrote it on a card: "Probably slower, less sun. I'd like to test it." At the fair a judge asked about cloudy days. Chidi smiled. He had a card for that.

qa.q: What did Chidi build the solar oven from?
qa.a: He built it out of a pizza box.

qa.q: How did Chidi feel when a judge asked about cloudy days?
qa.a: He felt confident and ready, smiling because he had prepared an answer.

qa.q: What else could Chidi do to prepare for questions he can't predict?
qa.a: He could practise admitting what he doesn't know and saying how he would test it, which judges respect.

qa.q: How does playing the mean judge look to Rafaela?
qa.a: Rafaela enjoys putting on a deep voice and helping, and her questions prepare her brother for the real judges.

grounding: It shows a boy rehearsing a one-minute explanation of his project and asking his sister to ask tricky questions to prepare for the judges.
